options: He may go home after finishing his work
He may go home after his work finished yesterday
He may go home finishing after work
He may go home to finish his work tomorrow
mcqs.why: Grammar B gives 'after finishing his work' as the adverb phrase replacing the clause 'after his work is finished'.

mcqs.q: State the kind of adverb clause: 'The player is out of the match because he has hurt himself.'
mcqs.why: Grammar C classifies 'because he has hurt himself' as an adverb clause of reason: it tells why the player is out of the match.

mcqs.q: State the kind of adverb clause: 'She switched on the television so that she could listen to the news.'
mcqs.why: Grammar C classifies 'so that she could listen to the news' as an adverb clause of purpose: it tells the purpose of switching on the television.

mcqs.q: State the kind of adverb clause: 'Where the road bends dangerously, be more careful.'
mcqs.why: Grammar C classifies 'Where the road bends dangerously' as an adverb clause of place, since it begins with 'where' and points to a place.

mcqs.q: Match the two clauses to make a meaningful sentence: 'You won't succeed' + ?
options: because the director did not show up
he went out without an umbrella
mcqs.why: Grammar D matches them as 4-a: 'You won't succeed if you don't try hard', a condition clause completing the main clause.

lessons.title: Writing Skills
lessons.notes_html:
Writing Skills

Q. (Writing A) Write a précis of paragraph 6 of the unit (model).

Ans. Précis (model): To feed the future generations adequately, population growth must be limited. Only a controlled number of people can be sustained by the land, water and energy resources. Sustaining the integrity of the ecosystem is therefore essential for a safe future.

Q. (Writing B) Write an essay on 'Over Population' (model, abridged).

Ans. Model essay: Over population is one of the most serious problems of the modern world, especially in developing countries like Pakistan. It puts great pressure on land, water, energy and food supplies and causes poverty, malnutrition and unemployment. Our resources are limited and are being depleted rapidly. The only solution is to control the growth of population through education and awareness, and to protect our ecosystem. A smaller, educated population can enjoy a better standard of life, while unchecked growth will make the future unsafe for our coming generations.

mcqs.q: The model précis of paragraph 6 says that, to feed the future generations adequately, ___ must be limited.
mcqs.why: Writing A opens with this point: to feed the future generations adequately, population growth must be limited.

mcqs.q: According to the précis, only a controlled number of people can be sustained by:
options: the land, water and energy resources
mcqs.why: Writing A states that only a controlled number of people can be sustained by the land, water and energy resources.

mcqs.q: The précis concludes that sustaining ___ is essential for a safe future.
mcqs.why: Writing A ends: sustaining the integrity of the ecosystem is therefore essential for a safe future.

mcqs.q: The model essay in Writing B is written on the topic:
mcqs.why: Writing B is the model essay on 'Over Population', one of the most serious problems of the modern world, especially in developing countries like Pakistan.

mcqs.q: According to the essay, over population puts great pressure on:
options: land, water, energy and food supplies
mcqs.why: Writing B lists land, water, energy and food supplies as the resources pressed by over population.

mcqs.q: The essay says over population causes:
mcqs.why: Writing B names poverty, malnutrition and unemployment as the results of unchecked population growth.

mcqs.q: The essay says our resources are limited and are being:
mcqs.why: Writing B warns that our resources are limited and are being depleted rapidly by the growing population.

mcqs.q: According to the essay, the only solution is to control population growth through:
options: education and awareness, and to protect our ecosystem
mcqs.why: Writing B gives the solution exactly so: control the growth of population through education and awareness, and protect the ecosystem.

mcqs.q: The essay says a smaller, educated population can enjoy:
mcqs.why: Writing B concludes that a smaller, educated population can enjoy a better standard of life.

mcqs.q: The essay warns that unchecked growth will make the future ___ for our coming generations.
mcqs.why: Writing B ends with this warning: unchecked growth will make the future unsafe for our coming generations.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Reading Comprehension

Q. (Reading 1) What case did the young men bring to Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA)?

Ans. The two young men brought the case of their father's murder. They dragged a villager before Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA) and accused him of killing their old father, demanding qisas (retribution) for the murder.

Q. (Reading 2) Why did the old man hurl a stone at the camel?

Ans. The villager's camel had entered the old man's garden and damaged his crops. In anger, the old man hurled a stone at the camel to drive it away, but the stone hit the camel so badly that it died on the spot.

Q. (Reading 3) Why did the villager ask Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA) to delay the execution?

Ans. The villager asked for a delay of three days because his father had left some gold for his younger brother, hidden in a place known only to him. He wanted to go home, hand over the gold to his brother and return, so that the trust (amanat) of his father would not be lost.

Q. (Reading 4) On what condition was the criminal allowed to leave?

Ans. The villager was allowed to leave on the condition that someone from the court stood surety (guarantor) for him and accepted that, if the villager did not return within three days, the surety himself would be executed in his place. Hazrat Abuzar Ghaffari (RA) accepted this surety.

Q. (Reading 5) Why were Sahabas (RA) worried?

Ans. The Sahabas (RA) were worried because the time of execution was near and the villager had not returned. They feared that Hazrat Abuzar Ghaffari (RA), a great companion of the Holy Prophet (PBUH), would be executed for the fault of an unknown villager.

Q. (Reading 6) Why did the accusers forgive the villager?

Ans. The accusers forgave the villager because he returned faithfully at the appointed time, although he could have run away and saved his life. His truthfulness and faithfulness touched their hearts, so they forgave him and withdrew their demand of qisas.

mcqs.q: What case did the two young men bring to Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA)?
options: They claimed the villager had stolen their camel
They accused a villager of killing their old father and demanded qisas (retribution)
They asked for a share in a garden
They complained about a land dispute
mcqs.why: Reading 1 states that the young men dragged a villager before Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA), accused him of killing their old father and demanded qisas for the murder.

mcqs.q: Why did the old man hurl a stone at the camel?
options: The camel had entered his garden and damaged his crops, and he wanted to drive it away
The camel had bitten his son
He wanted to kill the camel for its meat
The camel blocked the road to the city
mcqs.why: Reading 2 answers that the villager's camel entered the old man's garden and damaged his crops; in anger he hurled a stone to drive it away, but the camel died on the spot.

mcqs.q: Why did the villager ask Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA) to delay the execution?
options: He wanted to say farewell to his family
He hoped the accusers would change their minds
He was waiting for a witness to arrive
His father had left some gold for his younger brother, hidden in a place known only to him
mcqs.why: Reading 3 gives this reason: he wanted to hand over his father's hidden gold to his younger brother so that the trust (amanat) would not be lost.

mcqs.q: How many days’ delay did the villager request?
mcqs.why: Reading 3 and Reading 4 both fix the period at three days: he was to go home, hand over the gold and return within three days.

mcqs.q: On what condition was the villager allowed to leave?
options: He left his camel as a pledge
Someone from the court stood surety for him and accepted execution in his place if he did not return
He paid a heavy fine in advance
mcqs.why: Reading 4 states the condition exactly: a surety (guarantor) from the court would himself be executed if the villager did not return within three days.

mcqs.q: Who accepted the surety for the villager?
mcqs.why: Reading 4 records that Hazrat Abuzar Ghaffari (RA) accepted this surety, putting his own life at stake for an unknown villager.

mcqs.q: Why were the Sahabas (RA) worried as the time of execution drew near?
options: They doubted the justice of the decision
The accusers had left the city
The gold had been found by someone else
The villager had not returned, and they feared Hazrat Abuzar Ghaffari (RA) would be executed for the fault of an unknown villager
mcqs.why: Reading 5 explains their worry: the time of execution was near, the villager had not returned, and a great companion might be executed for a stranger's fault.

mcqs.q: Why did the accusers forgive the villager?
options: He paid them a large amount of gold
Hazrat Umar (RA) ordered them to forgive him
He returned faithfully at the appointed time although he could have run away, and his truthfulness touched their hearts
They found the real killer elsewhere
mcqs.why: Reading 6 answers that his faithful return, when he could have saved his life by running away, touched their hearts, so they forgave him.

mcqs.q: On forgiving the villager, the accusers withdrew their demand of:
mcqs.why: Reading 6 concludes that the accusers forgave him and withdrew their demand of qisas, so no execution took place.

mcqs.q: The hidden gold was a trust (amanat) left by the villager’s father for:
mcqs.why: Reading 3 states the father had left the gold for the villager's younger brother, hidden where only the villager knew; handing it over was his sacred trust.

lessons.title: Vocabulary
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary

Q. (Vocabulary A) 'To endanger' is a verb from 'danger'. Write down five verbs with the prefix 'en' and use these words in sentences.

Ans. (1) endanger: Reckless driving endangers the lives of others. (2) enable: This scholarship will enable her to complete her studies. (3) enrich: Reading good books enriches our minds. (4) ensure: Please ensure that the door is locked before leaving. (5) enlarge: They plan to enlarge the school library.

Q. (Vocabulary B) Explain the phrasal verbs and use them in sentences: take off, fell through, to hand over, bring in, come about, write down.

Ans. Take off — to remove; to leave the ground: The plane took off on time. Fell through — failed: Their plan fell through. To hand over — to give charge of: He handed over the gold to his brother. Bring in — to introduce/earn: The new law will bring in reforms. Come about — to happen: How did this accident come about? Write down — to note: Please write down your name and address.

Q. (Vocabulary C) Use as verb and as noun: fall, lead, control, grant, stand, mind, demand.

Ans. Fall (verb): Leaves fall in autumn. Fall (noun): The fall of the empire shocked everyone. Lead (verb): He will lead the team. Lead (noun): Our team took the lead. Control (verb): Control your anger. Control (noun): He lost control of the car. Grant (verb): The judge granted him bail. Grant (noun): The school received a grant. Stand (verb): Stand in a queue. Stand (noun): There is a bus stand nearby. Mind (verb): Mind your own business. Mind (noun): He has a sharp mind. Demand (verb): Workers demand higher wages. Demand (noun): Their demand is just.

Q. (Vocabulary D) Translate paragraph 5 of the unit into Urdu (model).

Ans. Model translation (of the paragraph in which the villager explains about his father's gold): ”اس نے کہا: اے امیر المؤمنین! میرے والد نے میرے چھوٹے بھائی کے لیے کچھ سونا چھوڑا تھا جو ایسی جگہ دفن ہے جسے میرے سوا کوئی نہیں جانتا۔ اگر مجھے قتل کر دیا گیا تو وہ سونا ضائع ہو جائے گا اور بھائی اپنے حق سے محروم رہ جائے گا۔ مجھے تین دن کی مہلت دی جائے تاکہ میں وہ امانت اس کے حوالے کر کے واپس آ جاؤں۔“

mcqs.q: The verb 'endanger' is formed from the noun 'danger' by adding the prefix:
mcqs.why: Vocabulary A begins from this example: 'to endanger' is a verb from 'danger' with the prefix en-, like enable, enrich, ensure and enlarge.

mcqs.q: Which en- verb completes the sentence: "This scholarship will ___ her to complete her studies"?
mcqs.why: Vocabulary A's model sentence uses 'enable': the scholarship will enable (make able) her to complete her studies.

mcqs.q: Which en- verb is used in the sentence: "Reading good books ___ our minds"?
mcqs.why: Vocabulary A gives 'enrich: Reading good books enriches our minds', meaning it makes the mind richer in knowledge.

mcqs.q: The phrasal verb 'fell through' means:
mcqs.why: Vocabulary B explains 'fell through' as failed, e.g. 'Their plan fell through', the opposite of what the villager's accusers expected of his promise.

mcqs.q: The phrasal verb 'take off', as used for a plane, means:
mcqs.why: Vocabulary B explains 'take off' as to remove, or (for a plane) to leave the ground: 'The plane took off on time.'

mcqs.q: The phrasal verb 'to hand over' means:
mcqs.why: Vocabulary B explains 'to hand over' as to give charge of, e.g. 'He handed over the gold to his brother', the villager's very purpose in the story.

mcqs.q: The phrasal verb 'come about' means:
mcqs.why: Vocabulary B explains 'come about' as to happen, as in the question 'How did this accident come about?'

mcqs.q: The phrasal verb 'write down' means:
mcqs.why: Vocabulary B explains 'write down' as to note: 'Please write down your name and address.'

mcqs.q: Which sentence uses 'lead' as a noun?
mcqs.why: Vocabulary C contrasts the two uses: 'He will lead the team' uses lead as a verb, while 'Our team took the lead' uses it as a noun.

mcqs.q: Which sentence uses 'grant' as a noun?
mcqs.why: Vocabulary C gives 'The school received a grant' as the noun use, while 'The judge granted him bail' uses grant as a verb.

lessons.title: Grammar
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar

Q. (Grammar A) Put in the correct verbs to make third conditional sentences: 1. If you ___ (not/be) late, we ___ (not/miss) the bus. 2. If we ___ (arrive) earlier, we ___ (see) our aunt. 3. If she ___ (go) to art school, she ___ (become) a painter. 4. If I ___ (be) born in a different country, I ___ (learn) to speak a different language. 5. They ___ (be) late if they ___ (not/take) a taxi. 6. We ___ (come) if we ___ (be) invited.

Ans. 1. If you had not been late, we would not have missed the bus. 2. If we had arrived earlier, we would have seen our aunt. 3. If she had gone to art school, she would have become a painter. 4. If I had been born in a different country, I would have learned to speak a different language. 5. They would have been late if they had not taken a taxi. 6. We would have come if we had been invited.

Q. (Grammar B) Combine the following sets of simple sentences to make compound sentences: 1. It rained for three days. The streets in my neighbourhood were flooded. 2. Kareem completed his homework. He put it in his binder. 3. Haris mowed the lawn. He earned hundred rupees. 4. Neelum doesn't like seafood. She doesn't like cabbage. 5. My pencil was broken. I borrowed one from Bushra. 6. I like apples. I like pears more. 7. Eight people got into the elevator. It was crowded. Three people got off. 8. Sara gathered the pictures. She could arrange them in a special album for her family.

Ans. 1. It rained for three days, so the streets in my neighbourhood were flooded. 2. Kareem completed his homework and put it in his binder. 3. Haris mowed the lawn and earned hundred rupees. 4. Neelum doesn't like seafood, nor does she like cabbage. 5. My pencil was broken, so I borrowed one from Bushra. 6. I like apples, but I like pears more. 7. Eight people got into the elevator, so it was crowded, and three people got off. 8. Sara gathered the pictures, so she could arrange them in a special album for her family.

Q. (Grammar C) Combine the following sets of simple sentences to make complex sentences: 1. I did not go to the meeting. I was sick. 2. You may be wrong. I cannot say. 3. He worked hard day and night. He did not wish to fail. 4. The examination ended. The students went home. 5. Their progress was slow. They were tired. 6. You should overlook his fault. It would be an act of generosity on your part. 7. We found him in the house. He had formerly lived in that house. 8. The boy gave an explanation of his misconduct. The explanation was not accepted by the headmaster.

Ans. 1. I did not go to the meeting because I was sick. 2. I cannot say whether you may be wrong. 3. He worked hard day and night because he did not wish to fail. 4. When the examination ended, the students went home. 5. Their progress was slow because they were tired. 6. It would be an act of generosity on your part if you overlooked his fault. 7. We found him in the house where he had formerly lived. 8. The boy gave an explanation of his misconduct which was not accepted by the headmaster.

Q. (Grammar D) Read the following sentences. Circle the subordinating conjunctions and use a comma where the dependent clause precedes the independent clause: 1. While I am attending school I can work part-time so that I can save money. 2. So that I could go to college my parents worked hard and saved money. 3. If the motor does not start we will have to find a mechanic as soon as possible. 4. Although the blue jacket was on sale I did not buy it. 5. When the school bell rang the children left the classroom. 6. Even after the fire was out there was a great deal of cleanup to do.

Ans. 1. While I am attending school, I can work part-time so that I can save money. (subordinating conjunctions: While, so that) 2. So that I could go to college, my parents worked hard and saved money. (So that) 3. If the motor does not start, we will have to find a mechanic as soon as possible. (If, as soon as) 4. Although the blue jacket was on sale, I did not buy it. (Although) 5. When the school bell rang, the children left the classroom. (When) 6. Even after the fire was out, there was a great deal of cleanup to do. (after)

Q. (Grammar E) Change from the direct into the indirect speech: The villager said, "I was leading my beloved camel ... and I surrendered myself to them."

Ans. The villager said that he had been leading his beloved camel. When he had reached a garden and halted to rest, the camel had nipped a few leaves off the hanging branch of a tree. The old man, on seeing this, had hurled a stone at the camel with all his might. The stone had caught the camel on the side of the head, and it had reeled and fallen down dead. He said that the camel had been very dear to him; he could not control his anger, so he had taken the same stone that had killed his dear camel and hurled it at the old man with all his strength, and it had hit the old man on the head and subsequently killed him. At this, those two young men had come to him and he had surrendered himself to them.

Q. (Grammar F) Rewrite each sentence, putting quotation marks at the appropriate places (interrupted quotations): 1. Do you think it's okay, asked Ali, if I wear this dress to school tomorrow? 2. If you had to guess, said Mr. Tariq, who would you say is my favourite author? 3. I will call you after I get home, Irum said, and we can discuss our science experiment together. 4. We'll be eating supper in about an hour, said mother, so don't eat any more snacks. 5. We need to fertilize the lawn today, said father, since it's supposed to rain tomorrow.

Ans. 1. "Do you think it's okay," asked Ali, "if I wear this dress to school tomorrow?" 2. "If you had to guess," said Mr. Tariq, "who would you say is my favourite author?" 3. "I will call you after I get home," Irum said, "and we can discuss our science experiment together." 4. "We'll be eating supper in about an hour," said mother, "so don't eat any more snacks." 5. "We need to fertilize the lawn today," said father, "since it's supposed to rain tomorrow."

mcqs.q: Make a third conditional sentence: 'If you ___ (not/be) late, we ___ (not/miss) the bus.'
options: had not been, would not have missed
had not been, will not miss
mcqs.why: Grammar A gives 'If you had not been late, we would not have missed the bus': third conditional = If + past perfect, would have + third form.

mcqs.q: Make a third conditional sentence: 'If she ___ (go) to art school, she ___ (become) a painter.'
mcqs.why: Grammar A gives 'If she had gone to art school, she would have become a painter', the third conditional form for an unreal past condition.

mcqs.q: Make a third conditional sentence: 'They ___ (be) late if they ___ (not/take) a taxi.'
options: would have been, had not taken
mcqs.why: Grammar A gives 'They would have been late if they had not taken a taxi': would have + third form in the main clause, past perfect in the if-clause.

mcqs.q: Make a third conditional sentence: 'We ___ (come) if we ___ (be) invited.'
options: would have come, had been invited
mcqs.why: Grammar A gives 'We would have come if we had been invited', with the passive past perfect 'had been invited' in the if-clause.

mcqs.q: The third conditional is formed as:
options: If + present indefinite, will + first form
If + past perfect, would have + third form of the verb
If + past indefinite, would + first form
mcqs.why: All six Grammar A sentences follow this pattern for unreal past conditions, e.g. 'If we had arrived earlier, we would have seen our aunt.'

mcqs.q: Combine into a compound sentence: 'Neelum doesn't like seafood. She doesn't like cabbage.'
options: Neelum doesn't like seafood, nor does she like cabbage.
Neelum doesn't like seafood because she doesn't like cabbage.
Neelum, who doesn't like cabbage, dislikes seafood.
Neelum doesn't like seafood when she dislikes cabbage.
mcqs.why: Grammar B joins them with 'nor' as a compound sentence: two independent clauses of equal rank, the second with inverted word order after 'nor'.

mcqs.q: Combine into a compound sentence: 'My pencil was broken. I borrowed one from Bushra.'
options: My pencil was broken because I borrowed one from Bushra.
My pencil, which was broken, I borrowed from Bushra.
Borrowing one from Bushra, my pencil was broken.
My pencil was broken, so I borrowed one from Bushra.
mcqs.why: Grammar B joins them with 'so', which shows the result: the broken pencil is the cause, borrowing one is the result.

mcqs.q: Combine into a compound sentence: 'I like apples. I like pears more.'
options: I like apples because I like pears more.
I like apples, which I like more than pears.
I like apples, but I like pears more.
Although I like apples, I like pears.
mcqs.why: Grammar B joins them with 'but' as a compound sentence, since the second clause contrasts with the first.

mcqs.q: Combine into a complex sentence: 'I did not go to the meeting. I was sick.'
options: I did not go to the meeting, so I was sick.
I did not go to the meeting because I was sick.
I did not go to the meeting and I was sick at home.
I was sick to the meeting.
mcqs.why: Grammar C joins them with 'because', making 'because I was sick' a subordinate clause of reason inside a complex sentence.

mcqs.q: Combine into a complex sentence: 'The examination ended. The students went home.'
options: When the examination ended, the students went home.
The examination ended, so the students went home.
The examination ended and the students at home.
The students went home to end the examination.
mcqs.why: Grammar C joins them with 'when', making a complex sentence with a subordinate clause of time placed before the main clause.

mcqs.q: Combine into a complex sentence: 'Their progress was slow. They were tired.'
options: Their progress was slow, so they were tired.
Their progress was slow and tired.
They were tired to make slow progress.
Their progress was slow because they were tired.
mcqs.why: Grammar C joins them with 'because': tiredness is the reason for the slow progress, expressed as a subordinate clause.

mcqs.q: The subordinating conjunctions in 'While I am attending school I can work part-time so that I can save money' are:
mcqs.why: Grammar D circles 'While' and 'so that' as the subordinating conjunctions, and punctuates: 'While I am attending school, I can work part-time so that I can save money.'

mcqs.q: When the dependent clause precedes the independent clause, it is followed by:
mcqs.why: Grammar D applies this rule throughout, e.g. 'When the school bell rang, the children left the classroom' and 'If the motor does not start, we will have to find a mechanic.'

mcqs.q: Choose the correct indirect speech: The villager said, "I was leading my beloved camel."
options: The villager said that he had been leading his beloved camel.
The villager said that he was leading my beloved camel.
The villager says that he is leading his camel.
The villager said I was leading his beloved camel.
mcqs.why: Grammar E changes the past continuous into the past perfect continuous and 'my' into 'his': the villager said that he had been leading his beloved camel.

mcqs.q: Which sentence punctuates the interrupted quotation correctly?
options: Do you think it’s okay, asked Ali, if I wear this dress to school tomorrow?
"Do you think it’s okay, asked Ali, if I wear this dress to school tomorrow"?
"Do you think it’s okay" asked Ali "if I wear this dress to school tomorrow?"
"Do you think it’s okay," asked Ali, "if I wear this dress to school tomorrow?"
mcqs.why: Grammar F punctuates it exactly so: each part of the interrupted quotation keeps its own quotation marks, with commas inside the closing marks.

lessons.title: Writing Skills
lessons.notes_html:
Writing Skills

Q. (Writing A) Write a character sketch of the villager (model).

Ans. Character sketch (model): The villager in the story is a true picture of faithfulness and honesty. He confessed his crime before Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA) and did not try to escape punishment. He cared more for his father's trust — the gold left for his younger brother — than for his own life. Although he was free for three days and could have run away, he returned at the appointed time and offered himself for execution. His truthfulness moved the hearts of his accusers, who forgave him. He teaches us that honesty and faithfulness always win respect and bring unexpected rewards.

Q. (Writing B) Summarize the story of Unit 13 with the help of a mind map — five main events (model).

Ans. Summary (model): 1. Two young men bring a villager to Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA), accusing him of killing their father, who had died after the villager's camel damaged his crops and he killed the camel with a stone — actually the old man died in the quarrel that followed. 2. The villager confesses and accepts the punishment of qisas. 3. He requests three days' delay to hand over his father's hidden gold to his younger brother. 4. Hazrat Abuzar Ghaffari (RA) stands surety for him, risking his own life. 5. The villager returns faithfully on the third day; the accusers, impressed by his faithfulness, forgive him, and Hazrat Abuzar (RA) is saved.

mcqs.q: According to the model character sketch, the villager confessed his crime before Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA) and:
options: asked for a pardon at once
did not try to escape punishment
mcqs.why: Writing A opens with this: the villager is a true picture of faithfulness and honesty; he confessed his crime and did not try to escape punishment.

mcqs.q: The sketch says the villager cared more for ___ than for his own life.
options: his father’s trust — the gold left for his younger brother
mcqs.why: Writing A states he cared more for his father's trust, the gold left for his younger brother, than for his own life.

mcqs.q: Although he was free for three days and could have run away, the villager:
options: sent the gold through a messenger
returned at the appointed time and offered himself for execution
mcqs.why: Writing A records this proof of his faithfulness: free for three days, he returned at the appointed time and offered himself for execution.

mcqs.q: His truthfulness moved the hearts of his accusers, who:
mcqs.why: Writing A concludes that his truthfulness moved the hearts of his accusers, who forgave him.

mcqs.q: The character sketch teaches us that honesty and faithfulness always:
options: win respect and bring unexpected rewards
save a man from all work
mcqs.why: Writing A closes with this lesson: honesty and faithfulness always win respect and bring unexpected rewards.

mcqs.q: In the model summary (Writing B), the first main event is:
options: Two young men bring a villager to Hazrat Umar Farooq (RA), accusing him of killing their father
The villager returns on the third day
mcqs.why: Writing B's five main events begin with the accusation: the young men bring the villager before Hazrat Umar (RA) for killing their father after the camel quarrel.

mcqs.q: In the summary, after confessing, the villager accepts the punishment of:
mcqs.why: Writing B's second event: the villager confesses and accepts the punishment of qisas (retribution) for the killing.

mcqs.q: In the summary, the villager requests three days’ delay in order to:
options: meet his family a last time
hand over his father’s hidden gold to his younger brother
mcqs.why: Writing B's third event: he requests three days' delay to hand over his father's hidden gold, the trust, to his younger brother.

mcqs.q: In the summary, who stands surety for the villager, risking his own life?
mcqs.why: Writing B's fourth event: Hazrat Abuzar Ghaffari (RA) stands surety for him, risking his own life if the villager failed to return.

mcqs.q: The summary ends with the villager returning faithfully on the third day, after which:
options: the accusers forgive him and Hazrat Abuzar (RA) is saved
the gold is divided among the Sahaba
mcqs.why: Writing B's fifth event: the villager returns faithfully on the third day; the accusers, impressed by his faithfulness, forgive him, and Hazrat Abuzar (RA) is saved.

lessons.title: Review Exercises
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar

Q. Change into passive voice: 'She wrote a letter.'

Ans. A letter was written by her. The object becomes the subject, 'was' is used with the third form 'written', and the doer is added with 'by'.

Vocabulary

Q. Give synonyms of 'just' and 'rapid' and an antonym of 'just'.

Ans. Just — fair, rightful; antonym — unjust. Rapid — quick, swift. Reviews revise the vocabulary of Units 1 to 4 in the same way.

True or False

True or False: The past indefinite tense is used for completed actions in the past. — True.

True or False: An abstract noun can be seen and touched. — False. An abstract noun names a quality, feeling or idea that cannot be seen or touched, e.g. justice, truthfulness and trust.

mcqs.q: Change into passive voice: 'She wrote a letter.'
options: A letter is written by her.
A letter was written by her.
A letter has being written by her.
mcqs.why: Review-I's grammar answer: the object 'a letter' becomes the subject, 'was' is used with the third form 'written', and the doer is added with 'by'.

mcqs.q: In the passive voice, which part of the active sentence becomes the subject?
mcqs.why: Review-I explains the change: the object becomes the subject, as 'a letter' becomes the subject of 'A letter was written by her.'

mcqs.q: For the past indefinite tense, the passive voice is formed with:
options: is/are + first form of the verb
has/have + second form of the verb
was/were + third form of the verb
mcqs.why: Review-I states that 'was' is used with the third form 'written' for this past indefinite sentence; 'were' serves plural subjects.

mcqs.q: In a passive sentence, the doer of the action is usually added with the preposition:
mcqs.why: Review-I notes that the doer is added with 'by', as in 'A letter was written by her.'

mcqs.q: Give a synonym of 'just':
mcqs.why: Review-I's vocabulary answer pairs 'just' with the synonyms fair and rightful; its antonym in the same answer is 'unjust'.

mcqs.q: Give an antonym of 'just':
mcqs.why: Review-I gives 'unjust' as the antonym of 'just', formed by adding the prefix un-, meaning not.

mcqs.q: Give a synonym of 'rapid':
mcqs.why: Review-I pairs 'rapid' with the synonyms quick and swift, both meaning fast.

mcqs.q: The past indefinite tense is used for:
mcqs.why: Review-I's True/False answer confirms this as True: the past indefinite tense is used for actions completed in the past.

mcqs.q: An abstract noun is a word for something that:
mcqs.why: Review-I's True/False answer marks 'An abstract noun can be seen and touched' as False: abstract nouns name qualities and ideas that cannot be seen or touched.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an abstract noun?
mcqs.why: Justice names a quality that cannot be seen or touched, so it is an abstract noun; letter, pen and table are concrete things, the contrast drawn in Unit 1's grammar and revised in this review.

lessons.title: Review Exercises
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar

Q. Identify the gerund and the infinitive: 'Reading is useful. He wants to read.'

Ans. 'Reading' is a gerund working as the subject. 'To read' is an infinitive working as the object of 'wants'.

Reading Comprehension

Q. What common quality do 'The Rain' and 'Peace' share?

Ans. Both texts end on a hopeful note. 'The Rain' hopes for sunshine after rain, and 'Peace' hopes for a world free of war through justice and dialogue.

True or False

True or False: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'. — True.

True or False: Personification gives human qualities to non-human things. — True.

mcqs.q: In 'Reading is useful', the word 'Reading' is:
options: an infinitive working as the object
a gerund working as the subject
mcqs.why: Review-II identifies 'Reading' as a gerund (the -ing form working as a noun) and it works as the subject of the sentence.

mcqs.q: In 'He wants to read', the words 'to read' are:
options: an infinitive working as the object of ‘wants’
a gerund working as the subject
mcqs.why: Review-II identifies 'to read' as an infinitive working as the object of 'wants', in contrast with the gerund in the first sentence.

mcqs.q: A gerund is:
options: the to + first form of a verb
the third form of a verb
the -ing form of a verb working as a noun
mcqs.why: Review-II's pair of sentences shows the gerund 'Reading' doing the work of a noun as subject, which is the defining feature of a gerund.

mcqs.q: An infinitive is:
options: the -ing form used as a noun
the past form of the verb
to + first form of the verb
mcqs.why: Review-II's example 'to read' shows the infinitive's form: 'to' plus the first form of the verb.

mcqs.q: What common quality do 'The Rain' and 'Peace' share?
options: Both texts end on a hopeful note
mcqs.why: Review-II's reading answer states this common quality: 'The Rain' hopes for sunshine after rain, and 'Peace' hopes for a world free of war.

mcqs.q: In 'The Rain', the poet hopes for ___ after the rain.
mcqs.why: Review-II explains the hope in 'The Rain' as sunshine after rain, just as joy follows sorrow in human life.

mcqs.q: 'Peace' hopes for a world free of war through:
mcqs.why: Review-II states that 'Peace' hopes for a world free of war through justice and dialogue instead of fighting.

mcqs.q: A simile compares two things using the words:
mcqs.why: Review-II's True/False answer confirms this as True: a simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as', e.g. 'He fought like a lion.'

mcqs.q: Personification is a figure of speech that:
options: gives human qualities to non-human things
uses a word in its dictionary sense
mcqs.why: Review-II's True/False answer confirms this definition as True: personification gives human qualities to non-human things.

mcqs.q: In 'The Rain', the sun shown as rising and smiling after the rain is an example of:
mcqs.why: Unit 5's grammar, revised in this review, names this personification: the sun, a non-human thing, is given the human quality of smiling.

lessons.title: Review Exercises
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar

Q. Change into indirect speech: Ali said, 'I have finished my work.'

Ans. Ali said that he had finished his work. The present perfect changes into the past perfect in indirect speech.

Writing Skills

Q. What is a précis? Give its rules in brief.

Ans. A précis is a short summary of a passage, usually one third of its length. It is written in one's own words, in the third person and in indirect speech, without adding any personal comments.

True or False

True or False: The second conditional shows an unreal present situation. — True.

True or False: In a précis we may add our own opinion about the passage. — False. A précis is a short summary written in one's own words; no personal comments or opinions may be added to it.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: Ali said, 'I have finished my work.'
options: Ali said that he has finished his work.
Ali said that he had finished his work.
Ali said that I have finished my work.
Ali says that he finishes his work.
mcqs.why: Review-III's grammar answer gives exactly this: the present perfect 'have finished' changes into the past perfect 'had finished' in indirect speech.

mcqs.q: In indirect speech, the present perfect tense changes into:
mcqs.why: Review-III explains the change in its answer: 'have finished' becomes 'had finished' when the reporting verb is in the past.

mcqs.q: A précis is:
options: a long essay on a topic
a short summary of a passage
mcqs.why: Review-III's writing answer defines a précis as a short summary of a passage, written in one's own words.

mcqs.q: A précis is usually ___ of the length of the original passage.
mcqs.why: Review-III states the rule: a précis is usually one third of the length of the original passage.

mcqs.q: A précis must be written in:
options: the exact words of the passage
mcqs.why: Review-III's rules require the précis to be written in one's own words, in the third person and in indirect speech.

mcqs.q: A précis is written in which person?
mcqs.why: Review-III lists this rule: a précis is written in the third person and in indirect speech, never as 'I' or 'you'.

mcqs.q: A précis is written in:
mcqs.why: Review-III's rules state that a précis is written in indirect speech, reporting the passage rather than quoting it.

mcqs.q: While writing a précis, we must NOT:
options: add our own opinion about the passage
mcqs.why: Review-III's True/False answer marks 'In a précis we may add our own opinion' as False: no personal comments may be added.

mcqs.q: The second conditional shows:
mcqs.why: Review-III's True/False answer confirms this as True: the second conditional, revised from Unit 10, shows an unreal present situation.

mcqs.q: The second conditional is formed as:
options: If + past indefinite, would + first form of the verb
If + past perfect, would have + third form
If + present indefinite, will + first form
mcqs.why: Unit 10's grammar, revised in this review, gives the form with examples like 'If I had wings, I would fly' and 'If we had no books, we would remain ignorant.'
